---
title: "Bayes' rule"
---

Suppose a pronunciation feature is strongly associated with a small dialect group. Hearing the feature may provide evidence about a speaker's dialect. But does a feature that is common within the group imply that most speakers who use the feature belong to the group? Not necessarily. The **conditional-direction problem** arises because the probability of group membership given the feature cannot be read directly from the probability of the feature given group membership.

Recall from [the chain rule](probability-factorization.qmd) that the same joint probability can be factored in two orders:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
=\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
=\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

The left sides name the same intersection. Thus the right sides are equal:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)
=\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

We want the conditional probability with $C$ to the right of the bar. If $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$, divide both sides by $\mathbb{P}(C)$:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B)}
       {\mathbb{P}(C)}.
$$

This identity is [**Bayes' rule**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html). Basically, it reverses the direction of a conditional probability while correcting for the two marginal probabilities. More specifically, it follows from applying the chain rule to one joint probability in two orders. No independence assumption is used.

## The pronoun measure

Let $A_4$ be the accusative event and $P_4$ the plural event in $\Omega_4$. We want $\mathbb{P}(A_4\mid P_4)$. Bayes' rule gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(A_4\mid P_4)
=\frac{\mathbb{P}(P_4\mid A_4)\mathbb{P}(A_4)}
       {\mathbb{P}(P_4)}.
$$

The values from the joint table are

$$
\mathbb{P}(P_4\mid A_4)=\frac{.40}{.70},
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(A_4)=.70,
\qquad
\mathbb{P}(P_4)=.50.
$$

Substituting them gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(A_4\mid P_4)
&=\frac{(.40/.70)\times.70}{.50}\\
&=\frac{.40}{.50}\\
&=.80.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is the same value obtained from the definition of conditional probability. Bayes' rule computes it from the reversed conditional probability and the two marginal probabilities.

## A dialect-feature example

Now let $D$ be membership in a dialect group and $F$ be use of a pronunciation feature. The table below is a hypothetical teaching example; it does not report a real dialect or establish that a feature diagnoses group membership. Imagine a represented population of 1,000 tokens with these counts.

| | feature $F$ | no feature $F^c$ | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| dialect group $D$ | 90 | 10 | 100 |
| other group $D^c$ | 180 | 720 | 900 |
| total | 270 | 730 | 1,000 |

Within the dialect group, the feature is very common:

$$
\mathbb{P}(F\mid D)=\frac{90}{100}=.90.
$$

We want the reversed probability, the probability of group membership given the feature:

$$
\mathbb{P}(D\mid F).
$$

The other required values are

$$
\mathbb{P}(D)=\frac{100}{1000}=.10
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(F)=\frac{270}{1000}=.27.
$$

Bayes' rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(D\mid F)
&=\frac{\mathbb{P}(F\mid D)\mathbb{P}(D)}
        {\mathbb{P}(F)}\\
&=\frac{.90\times.10}{.27}\\
&=\frac{1}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now pause at the apparent discrepancy. The feature occurs in ninety percent of the dialect-group tokens, but only one third of all tokens containing the feature come from that group. The group accounts for only ten percent of the population, and the feature also occurs outside the group. Both facts enter the reversed conditional probability.

```{r}
#| eval: false
p_feature_given_dialect <- .90
p_dialect <- .10
p_feature <- .27

p_dialect_given_feature <-
  p_feature_given_dialect * p_dialect / p_feature

p_dialect_given_feature
```

The result is approximately `.333`.

## Evidence and prevalence

In the dialect calculation, $\mathbb{P}(F\mid D)$ gives the probability of the feature within the group, $\mathbb{P}(D)$ gives the prevalence of the group in the represented population, and $\mathbb{P}(F)$ gives the overall probability of the feature.

All three quantities are tied to an observation process. A sample balanced to contain equal numbers of speakers from two groups does not directly provide the population value of $\mathbb{P}(D)$. Using the sample proportion would answer a question about the balanced sample unless the design is adjusted to represent the target population. And token counts do not by themselves state how the pattern varies across speakers, styles, or speaking situations.

## The order of the events

As discussed in the [introduction to conditional probability](conditional-probability.qmd#the-order-of-the-events), $\mathbb{P}(F\mid D)$ cannot be substituted for $\mathbb{P}(D\mid F)$. Bayes' rule shows exactly what that substitution omits: the prevalence of $D$ and the overall probability of $F$.

A feature may be common within a rare group even though most tokens containing that feature come from elsewhere. We can verify the direction of the conditional in the count table: $90/270$ is the proportion of feature tokens from the dialect group, while $90/100$ is the proportion of dialect-group tokens containing the feature.

The exact upshot is that reversing a conditional requires both the original direction and the relevant marginal probabilities. The [next page](independence.qmd) asks when conditioning leaves a probability unchanged, so that one of these corrections becomes unnecessary.

## Check your understanding

1. Derive Bayes' rule by equating the two chain-rule factorizations of $\mathbb{P}(B,C)$.
2. In the dialect table, compute $\mathbb{P}(F\mid D^c)$ and $\mathbb{P}(D^c\mid F)$.
3. Explain in words why $.90$ and $1/3$ answer different questions.
4. If the dialect group made up half of the represented population while the two within group feature rates stayed fixed, would $\mathbb{P}(D\mid F)$ increase or decrease? Explain without introducing a new formula.
